The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **complex measure** on
$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathbb C$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   in $\mathbb C$.

The codomain is the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]), so a complex measure is finite-valued by
definition: there is no complex number called $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ to allow.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then
$|\nu|$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Because
$|\nu|$ is a measure ([[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]]), define
$$L^1(\nu):=L^1(|\nu|)$$
using the published meaning of $L^1$ from [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]].

If $f\in L^1(\nu)$, choose complex simple functions $s_n$ as in
[[thm-l-one-functions-admit-dominated-complex-simple-approximations]] with
$\int |f-s_n|\,d|\nu|\to0$. The simple-integral bound
[[prop-simple-integrals-are-bounded-by-total-variation]] makes
$(\int s_n\,d\nu)$ a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb C$, and its limit is
independent of the chosen approximating sequence. Define
$$\int f\,d\nu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int s_n\,d\nu.$$

For a measurable set $E\in\mathcal A$, define
$$\int_E f\,d\nu:=\int f\mathbf 1_E\,d\nu.$$

$f\in L^1(
u)$. Then

uight|\le \int |f|\,d|
u|.$$
More generally, for every measurable $E$,

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Choose a countable measurable partition $(E_n)_{n\ge0}$ of $\mathcal X$ with $\mu(E_n)<\infty$ by disjointifying a sigma-finite cover [F2]. Put $c_n=2^{-(n+1)}/(1+\mu(E_n))$ and $\lambda(A)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n\mu(A\cap E_n)$. For disjoint measurable $A_m$, countable additivity of $\mu$ and interchange of nonnegative double series give $\lambda(\bigcup_m A_m)=\sum_n c_n\sum_m\mu(A_m\cap E_n)=\sum_m\lambda(A_m)$; the interchange is valid because both sides are the supremum of the same finite subsums. Thus $\lambda$ is a measure. Also $\lambda(\mathcal X)\le\sum_{n\ge0}2^{-(n+1)}=1$. Since every $c_n>0$, $\lambda(A)=0$ iff every $\mu(A\cap E_n)=0$, iff $\mu(A)=0$. Thus $\lambda$ is finite and equivalent to $\mu$, so every $P_\theta\ll\lambda$.

For each $\theta$, choose the RN density $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\lambda$ from [F3], finite outside a $\lambda$-null set, and let $A_\theta=\{p_\theta>0\}$. Fix $\theta_*$; since $\int p_{\theta_*}\,d\lambda=1$, $\lambda(A_{\theta_*})>0$. Define $s=\sup_{F\subseteq\Theta,\,F\text{ finite}}\lambda(\bigcup_{\theta\in F}A_\theta)$, so $0<s\le\lambda(\mathcal X)<\infty$. By [A1], choose finite $F_n$ for each $n\ge0$ with union measure greater than $s-1/(n+1)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, these unions have positive measure, so the selected index set $\bigcup_nF_n$ is nonempty. Set $A=\bigcup_n\bigcup_{\theta\in F_n}A_\theta$. Finite unions from the selected sets have measure at most $s$, so [F4] applied to their indicators gives $\lambda(A)\le s$ by continuity from below; the approximations give $\lambda(A)\ge s$. Hence $\lambda(A)=s$.

Fix $\theta$. If $\lambda(A_\theta\setminus A)>0$, the increasing finite unions $(\bigcup_{n\le N}\bigcup_{\phi\in F_n}A_\phi)\cup A_\theta$ converge to $A\cup A_\theta$, whose measure is greater than $s$. [F4] applied to their indicators shows that some finite union then exceeds $s$, contradicting its definition. Therefore $p_\theta=0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on $A^c$.

Enumerate the nonempty countable collection of selected indices $\bigcup_nF_n$ as $(\theta_j)$, allowing repetitions if needed, and choose positive weights summing to one. The mixture $Q=\sum_jw_jP_{\theta_j}$ has density $q=\sum_jw_jp_{\theta_j}$ by [F4], so $q>0$ exactly on $A$ up to a $\lambda$-null set. If $Q(C)=0$, then $\int_Cq\,d\lambda=0$. For each $m\ge1$, $\lambda(C\cap A\cap\{q\ge1/m\})/m\le\int_Cq\,d\lambda=0$; these sets cover $C\cap A$ up to the null set where $q$ is not positive on $A$. Hence $\lambda(C\cap A)=0$. Also every $p_\theta$ vanishes on $A^c$ by step 3.1, so $P_\theta(C)=\int_Cp_\theta d\lambda=0$. Since $\theta$ was arbitrary, $P_\theta\ll Q$ for all $\theta$.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. $$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. $$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Let $\mathcal X$ be countable with its full $\sigma$-field, so it is standard Borel under the discrete metric. Let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be dominated by a fixed $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$. Choose the finite-valued densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ as in [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let $X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ satisfy $P_\theta(X_0)=1$ and $P_\theta(\{x\})>0$ for every $x\in X_0$ and every $\theta$. Write $m_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. For each $x\in X_0$, $0<\mu(\{x\})<\infty$ and $p_\theta(x)=m_\theta(x)/\mu(\{x\})$: positivity follows from $m_\theta(x)>0$, finiteness from sigma-finiteness, and the value is fixed by the density integral on the positive-measure singleton. Consequently

$$\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(y)}=\frac{m_\theta(x)}{m_\theta(y)}\frac{\mu(\{y\})}{\mu(\{x\})}.$$

For $x,y\in X_0$, define $x\sim y$ if there is a constant $c(x,y)>0$ such that $m_\theta(x)/m_\theta(y)=c(x,y)$ for every $\theta$. The displayed fixed singleton factor shows this is equivalent to constancy of the common-reference density ratio. This is an equivalence relation: the constants for $(x,x)$, $(y,x)$ and $(x,z)$ are respectively $1$, $c(x,y)^{-1}$ and $c(x,y)c(y,z)$. Its equivalence classes form a countable quotient. Equip that quotient with its discrete $\sigma$-field; it is standard Borel because the discrete metric is complete and the countable space itself is dense. Since $\Theta\ne\varnothing$ and $P_\theta(X_0)=1$, $X_0$ is nonempty; define the class statistic by mapping each point of $X_0$ to its class and every point off $X_0$ to any fixed class. It is measurable because $\mathcal X$ has the full $\sigma$-field, and values off $X_0$ are null under every law.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

A statistic $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is **complete** for $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ if, for every measurable real-valued $g$ such that $E_\theta|g(T)|<\infty$ for every $\theta$, the conditions $E_\theta[g(T)]=0$ for every $\theta$ imply $P_\theta(g(T)=0)=1$ for every $\theta$. Integrability is part of the premise; completeness is a property of the statistic relative to the specified family.

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom

recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and set $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Assume $P_\theta\ll P_0$ for every $\theta$. Then $T$ is sufficient if and only if for every $\theta$ the Radon–Nikodym derivative $dP_\theta/dP_0$ has a $\sigma(T)$-measurable version. Equivalently, for each $\theta$ there is a Borel $g_\theta:\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty)$ with $dP_\theta/dP_0=g_\theta(T)$ $P_0$-almost surely. The null exceptional set may depend on $\theta$. The requirement $P_0\in\{P_\theta\}$ is essential; an arbitrary external dominating probability is not covered.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

   ([[def-linear-subspace]]) is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(W) = 0$.

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. Assume AC and let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be a full-rank exponential family as in [[def-exponential-family]], with $\Omega$ containing a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$. Then its canonical statistic $T$ is complete.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, and let $T$ and $U$ be statistics from this sample space into standard Borel spaces for a family $(P_\theta)$. If $T$ is complete and sufficient and $U$ is ancillary, then $T$ and $U$ are independent under every $P_\theta$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

derivations.claim: The mean map is continuous, hence Borel by [F2] and a statistic. Use $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $dx$ as base measure; it is sigma-finite by [F3]. By [F1] and the translation case of [F10], each coordinate has density $\phi(x_i-\mu)$. Independence [F4] gives the product joint law. For $n=1$ this is already the joint density. For $n\ge2$, repeated use of [F13] identifies $\lambda_n$ with the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. The measure with density $q(x)=\prod_i\phi(x_i-\mu)$ relative to $\lambda_n$ exists by [F11]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] and the rectangle formula [F12] show that its values on Borel rectangles are the products of the marginal probabilities; [F14] says these rectangles generate the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^n$, so repeated product-measure uniqueness [F12] identifies it with the joint law. Thus $p_\mu(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_i x_i^2+\mu\sum_i x_i-\tfrac n2\mu^2)$. Setting $T=\bar X$, $\eta=n\mu$, and $h(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-\sum_i x_i^2/2}$ writes it as $h(x)e^{\eta T(x)-A(\eta)}$ with $A(\eta)=\eta^2/(2n)$. Completing the square and using Tonelli gives $\int h e^{\eta T}dx=e^{\eta^2/(2n)}$. The natural parameter set is all $\mathbb R$, hence open. For $b\ne0$, the level set $b\bar x=c$ is a proper affine hyperplane, null by [F3], so $T$ has no affine constraint; it is full rank by [F5]. The residual map $x\mapsto x-\bar x\mathbf1$ is continuous, hence a statistic by [F2]. Write $X_i=\mu+Z_i$ with iid $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ by [F1]. Then $R_i=Z_i-\bar Z$, so the law of $R$ does not depend on $\mu$; it is ancillary by [F8]. Apply [F9] to conclude $\bar X$ and $R$ are independent under every $P_\mu$.

Let $\mathcal X$ be countable with its full $\sigma$-field, so it is standard Borel under the discrete metric. Let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be dominated by a fixed $\sigma$-finite positive measure $\mu$. Choose the finite-valued densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$ as in [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let $X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ satisfy $P_\theta(X_0)=1$ and $P_\theta(\{x\})>0$ for every $x\in X_0$ and every $\theta$. Write $m_\theta(x)=P_\theta(\{x\})$. For each $x\in X_0$, $0<\mu(\{x\})<\infty$ and $p_\theta(x)=m_\theta(x)/\mu(\{x\})$: positivity follows from $m_\theta(x)>0$, finiteness from sigma-finiteness, and the value is fixed by the density integral on the positive-measure singleton. Consequently

$$\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(y)}=\frac{m_\theta(x)}{m_\theta(y)}\frac{\mu(\{y\})}{\mu(\{x\})}.$$

For $x,y\in X_0$, define $x\sim y$ if there is a constant $c(x,y)>0$ such that $m_\theta(x)/m_\theta(y)=c(x,y)$ for every $\theta$. The displayed fixed singleton factor shows this is equivalent to constancy of the common-reference density ratio. This is an equivalence relation: the constants for $(x,x)$, $(y,x)$ and $(x,z)$ are respectively $1$, $c(x,y)^{-1}$ and $c(x,y)c(y,z)$. Its equivalence classes form a countable quotient. Equip that quotient with its discrete $\sigma$-field; it is standard Borel because the discrete metric is complete and the countable space itself is dense. Since $\Theta\ne\varnothing$ and $P_\theta(X_0)=1$, $X_0$ is nonempty; define the class statistic by mapping each point of $X_0$ to its class and every point off $X_0$ to any fixed class. It is measurable because $\mathcal X$ has the full $\sigma$-field, and values off $X_0$ are null under every law.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses of [[def-likelihood-ratio-equivalence-on-common-discrete-support]], let $T(x)=[x]_{\sim}$ on $X_0$, as a statistic into the countable quotient with its discrete standard-Borel structure, and assign one arbitrary class off $X_0$. Then $T$ is minimal sufficient for $(P_\theta)$, modulo $\mathcal X\setminus X_0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Every sample point has probability $m_p(x)=p^{t(x)}(1-p)^{n-t(x)}>0$, so the common support is the whole finite sample space. Counting measure assigns mass one to each point, so the densities equal these point masses; for $x,y$, their ratio is $m_p(x)/m_p(y)=[p/(1-p)]^{t(x)-t(y)}$.

If $t(x)=t(y)$, this ratio is one for all $p$. If $d=t(x)-t(y)\ne0$, its values at $p=1/2$ and $p=1/3$ are respectively $1$ and $(1/2)^d$, which differ. Thus equivalence classes are exactly the level sets of $T$. By [F2], $T$ is minimal sufficient.

Minimality is modulo sets null under every model law. It does not assert literal pointwise equality with any other minimal sufficient statistic.
